555.bp: When a lie spreads on Twitter, Facebook, or TikTok, it gets shared millions of times before anyone stops it. Understanding how many people will interact with false information—will they like, comment, or repost it—matters because platforms need to decide which warnings to show and where to spend moderation effort. The speed and shape of that engagement tells us whether a lie is about to explode.
555.wh: The obvious approach treats engagement numbers as just numbers over time: 'This post got 100 likes yesterday, 50 today, maybe 30 tomorrow.' But that misses the real game. Users aren't mindless; they're making deals with each other. When you share misinformation, you're trading your reputation or effort for social status, connection, or validation. Different platforms reward different behaviors, so the engagement pattern on TikTok looks nothing like Reddit. A pure time-series model has no idea what that psychology is.
555.ap: This work builds a neural system that watches 2.37 million posts across seven platforms and learns to decode the unwritten social contracts at play. Instead of treating engagement as a sequence of numbers, it models each action as a moment in an exchange: 'This user is now choosing to comment—that costs them time but buys them visibility.' The system learns how emotions (anger travels differently than sadness) and platform quirks (TikTok's algorithm versus Twitter's timeline) reshape what people do next. As time unfolds, the model tracks how the negotiation between user effort and social reward shifts.
555.ww: When you realize that engagement is not chaos but negotiation, you can predict it. A viral moment isn't random—it's that sweet spot where the social reward (everyone's cheering) outweighs the effort (sharing a false claim). By learning the principles of that trade-off from the data itself, the system stops relying on hand-coded rules and instead discovers what actually drives people on each platform.
555.po: On real posts, the system predicts engagement with 19.25% error on average—43.6% better than previous best methods. That means when a misinformation post appears, the platform can now estimate how far it will spread with much higher confidence, enabling faster intervention and smarter resource allocation where it matters most.

556.bp: Every day, millions of users click products on Alibaba, report fraud to PayPal, or browse Netflix. These happen in a stream—data arrives one user at a time, never stops, and tomorrow's patterns might not match today's. A good AI system has to learn from this endless flow and stay sharp even when the world shifts. Most systems work like students who study once and never adapt, but stream learning is about studying while the exam is happening.
556.wh: The problem is twofold and vicious. First, redundancy: most incoming data repeats what you already know, so you waste training cycles on useless examples. Second, catastrophic forgetting: if you update your system on only new data, you forget how to handle old cases—like learning a new language and forgetting your native tongue overnight. Picking which samples to study and which old knowledge to keep is hard when you don't have time to recompute scores for everything.
556.ap: Instead of recomputing everything from scratch, this work introduces fingerprints—compact summaries that capture 'what does this model currently know?' Think of a fingerprint as a tiny portrait of the model's brain state. When a new example arrives, you compare its fingerprint to the model's fingerprint and ask: 'How similar are we?' That score tells you two things at once: should I learn this new example (coreset selection), and should I forget some old example to make room (buffer update)? A small plugin powered by pre-trained vision transformers fine-tunes these fingerprints without heavy computation.
556.ww: Fingerprints work because they're a middle ground between lazy and costly. Rule-based systems can't adapt when patterns shift. Gradient-based systems require computing derivatives for every example, which is slow. Fingerprints are fast (just a dot product) but smart (they learn what patterns matter). Because they're learnable and lightweight, the system can stay responsive to change without grinding to a halt.
556.po: This framework lets streaming AI systems learn efficiently in real-time applications. When deployed on live recommendation or fraud-detection tasks, it picks the most useful examples to learn and preserves critical historical patterns, improving both accuracy and speed compared to naive approaches that either learn everything or forget everything.

557.bp: Graph anomaly detection is everywhere: a cybersecurity team needs to spot hackers hiding in network traffic, a bank needs to find fraudsters in a transaction network, Google needs to find spam in its web graph. Anomalies are rare and weird by definition, so you can't just build a detector on a clean dataset and deploy it to a messy real graph. It has to generalize to new graphs it has never seen before.
557.wh: Two approaches sound reasonable but both fail. First: learn one big model that transfers across graphs (domain transfer). The catch is that anomalies don't transfer—a botnet in one network looks different than a botnet in another. Second: build separate models for each domain that handle multiple tasks together (multi-task learning). But then you need a labeled example from the new domain first, and in real deployment, you don't have that. The two challenges—cross-domain transfer and detecting rare anomalies—seem to pull in opposite directions.
557.ap: This system builds a foundation model—a universal pretrained detector—but trains it in an unsupervised way (no labels needed). The trick is synthetic generation: the model learns normal behavior from clean data, then uses adversarial techniques to invent fake anomalies it has never seen before. This way, it gets exposure to diverse anomalies without anyone having to hand-label rare events. At test time on a new unseen graph, it freezes the backbone (keeps the core logic) and only fine-tunes the detection head, letting it adapt quickly to that specific domain.
557.ww: By learning to generate anomalies synthetically, the model avoids the rare-event problem: you don't have to wait for anomalies to naturally occur in your training set, and you don't have to label them manually. By training once on a single dataset but generating diverse fake anomalies, the model learns general principles of 'what makes something weird' that travel across domains. Freezing the backbone at test time keeps it from forgetting those principles when it adapts to new data.
557.po: The system can now detect anomalies at multiple levels (individual nodes, connections, subgraph clusters) on graphs it has never encountered before, without any labeled examples from those new domains. This cuts months off deployment: you no longer need to label anomalies in each new graph; the pretrained system can go to work immediately and adapt.

558.bp: Every second, ads compete in an auction. A shampoo company bids on ad slots on Google, an e-commerce seller bids on TikTok. The bidding happens in microseconds and the goal is simple: spend your budget wisely to reach your customers. Doing this well by hand is impossible at scale, so auto-bidding systems make those split-second decisions. A bad strategy wastes money; a good one reaches the right customer at the right price.
558.wh: Current auto-bidding systems learn from historical auction data using reinforcement learning or pattern matching. The problem: they're black boxes. When they bid \\$50 for an ad, nobody—not even the system—can explain why, and sometimes the decisions look absurd because the training data was limited in what it had seen. You also have to manually code the rules for how auctions work. Large language models sound like they could help because they're good at reasoning and explaining, but they can hallucinate—making up facts or bids that make no sense in a real auction.
558.ap: This work puts an LLM in charge but in a clever, two-layer way. The first layer (LBM-Think) is a reasoning engine: the LLM reads the auction situation and thinks out loud about strategy. 'The user is high-value, the auction is competitive, I should bid up.' This stays in words and logic, grounded. The second layer (LBM-Act) takes that reasoning and converts it to precise numerical bids. To make these two layers understand each other, the system uses dual embeddings: one for words and one for numbers, fused together so reasoning and action are tight partners.
558.ww: Separating thinking from action breaks the hallucination problem. The thinking layer can reason, but it doesn't directly control the bid; the action layer translates reasoning into numbers and can validate that bids make sense for the auction. The dual embedding ensures the reasoning and action layers are pulling in the same direction, not working against each other. Because the reasoning is in plain language, the system is also transparent—you can see why it bid what it bid.
558.po: Auto-bidding systems now make decisions that are both competitive (winning auctions) and explainable (humans can see the reasoning). The system can also generalize to new auction types because its reasoning layer has learned general principles from language, not just memorized patterns in old data.

559.bp: Events happen in the world—a political scandal emerges, a celebrity dies, a stock crashes. These events cascade across platforms and modalities: text discusses them, images spread them, videos explain them. To forecast what will happen next—will a disaster escalate, will a trend die, will a stock recover—you need to understand how information moves and changes shape as it flows across text, images, and knowledge networks. No single modality tells the whole story.
559.wh: The obvious step: pile up text features, image features, and relationship graphs, then mash them together in one model. But the temporal aspect breaks this. A tweet's meaning shifts over time, and early tweets matter more for forecasting than late ones. Images have different time sensitivities than text. And relationships in a knowledge graph—'person A is related to person B'—have their own temporal structure. Existing methods glue text and images together in static ways and don't learn how each modality's temporal behavior shapes the final forecast.
559.ap: This system learns from four angles at once. First, it extracts time-sensitive information from three geometric spaces—Euclidean (straightforward distance), hyperbolic (tree-like relationships), and complex (cyclic patterns)—to capture deep, multi-level connections in knowledge graphs. Pretrained models supply time-aware linguistic and visual features. Second, instead of asking 'how much does each modality matter,' it asks 'how does each modality's importance shift over time?' It learns adaptive weights that realize different modalities lead the forecast at different moments: early text might matter more, then images become critical, then the graph relationships reassert themselves.
559.ww: By using multiple geometric spaces, the system can capture relationships at different levels of abstraction—hierarchies, cycles, simple distances—that happen naturally in real data. By learning time-varying modality weights, it stops forcing false equality: not all modalities are equally important at each moment. This combination lets the system ride the temporal currents of real-world events, where information flows and transforms across modalities in complex, time-dependent ways.
559.po: On real multimodal event data spanning text, images, and knowledge graphs, the system forecasts future events more accurately than methods that treat modalities equally or statically. This enables better predictions of how world events will unfold, from crisis escalation to market movements.

560.bp: Traffic flow is one of the clearest examples of patterns hidden in space and time. Congestion spreads from car to car, street to street, and the spread follows geography, not just sequence. A road network is not a line—it's a web where traffic on one street affects neighbors nearby. To predict delays before they happen and reroute traffic intelligently, a system must understand both the temporal rhythm (rush hour builds to a peak) and the spatial spreading (blockage propagates along connected roads).
560.wh: LLMs excel at sequential patterns—they read text left to right and predict what comes next. Traffic is different: the most important spatial neighbors aren't in sequence, they're geographically nearby. An LLM trained on traffic as a sequence will miss that non-sequential spatial structure entirely. It will learn temporal rhythms well but blind itself to how congestion actually spreads across the road network.
560.ap: This system starts with an LLM but patches it with two adaptations. First, it freezes part of the LLM (Partially Frozen Attention) to preserve the temporal reasoning the LLM learned during pretraining, then strategically unfreezes and retrains the attention mechanism to respond to new traffic data. Second, it embeds the road network's adjacency structure directly into the attention mask—a clever trick that forces attention to respect geography. When computing attention, spatially connected nodes can interact directly, regardless of where they fall in a sequence. A fine-tuning method called DoRA does this adaptation stably without destabilizing the model.
560.ww: By embedding geography into attention, the system gets spatial reasoning for free without completely rewriting the model. The frozen component preserves the temporal logic learned from diverse pretraining data. The unfrozen component learns traffic-specific spatial patterns. This hybrid approach avoids both extremes: a fully retrained model that forgets general temporal reasoning, and an untouched LLM that ignores spatial structure.
560.po: Traffic forecasting improves because the system now captures the full two-dimensional reality: how patterns roll forward in time and how congestion ripples across the connected road network. Real-world traffic data shows this beats methods that handle only temporal or only spatial patterns.

561.bp: A financial network shifts when markets close overnight. A social graph changes when new users join. A security graph evolves as attacks evolve. Real-world graphs are rarely static, and they're never pure. They're full of noise and variation—patterns that belong to the specific data distribution you're looking at, not universal truths. A detector trained on one bank's transaction graph will fail on another bank's graph because the patterns it learned were specific to the first bank, not general rules about fraud.
561.wh: Out-of-distribution detection is hard even in flat data. But graphs add complexity: not only does the overall distribution shift, but the structure itself might differ—one graph is densely connected, another is sparse. Two competing goals seem incompatible: generalize across domains (ignore domain-specific noise) while also detect anomalies (catch rare, weird cases that look different from the norm). Anomalies are inherently out-of-distribution by definition, so a system optimized to ignore distribution shift might miss them entirely.
561.ap: This work proposes a unified framework that tackles both goals with three components. First, a generator that models which subgraphs are normal in each data distribution—without needing labels—by learning conditional distributions. Second, a spectral contrastive learning module that learns what's invariant (stays true across domains) versus what's shifting (domain-specific noise). Third, an approach to integrate labeled and unlabeled data using principles of invariance so that learning from labeled examples in one domain helps with unlabeled data in another. The system learns to extract the stable patterns that matter and discard the shifting noise.
561.ww: By learning invariant subgraphs without labels, the system avoids the bottleneck of needing labeled anomalies in every domain—they're rare, and labeling them is expensive. By treating generalization and detection as two sides of the same coin (both need to spot what's truly invariant), the system avoids the false choice between the two. Spectral methods (analyzing the structure of the graph mathematically) naturally expose both the stable core and the shifting periphery.
561.po: The system detects anomalies at multiple levels (node, edge, subgraph) in new graphs without labeled training data from those graphs. By learning what's truly invariant across domains, it becomes more reliable when deployed to real but messy data where distributions drift constantly.

562.bp: Diffusion models—systems that generate images or text by reversing noise—have become powerful tools. But they can be misused: someone could fine-tune a model to generate harmful imagery or synthesize deepfakes. Once a diffusion model is released for public use or deployed locally, the creator loses control. The question is: how do you enforce safety rules on a model you no longer physically control?
562.wh: Traditional safety measures—filtering outputs, blocking certain keywords—happen at the end of generation and are easy to bypass by clever prompting. They also require retraining or reconfiguring the entire model each time a new safety concern emerges. If someone fine-tunes your model locally with their own data, your safety guardrails evaporate. There's no mechanism for a third-party regulator to enforce rules on a model running someone else's machine.
562.ap: This system proposes a tripartite setup: the model creator, the users (who might fine-tune locally), and a third-party regulator. The regulator embeds special regulatory signatures and regulatory layers into the model at release time. These layers act like embedded sensors and controllers. During both fine-tuning and sampling, the regulator monitors intermediate steps and injects regulatory signals that steer the model away from unsafe outputs. The regulatory layers are tightly coupled with the signatures so that the regulator can influence the sampling process with minimal overhead, even on a model running far away.
562.ww: By moving regulation to intermediate steps rather than the final output, the system stops workarounds: you can't just rephrase to bypass it. By coupling regulatory layers with the model at creation time and making them tight to the model's internal logic, the regulator's influence is baked in and harder to disable. The regulator doesn't need to retrain the model each time; different signature types trigger different regulatory behaviors.
562.po: Unsafe outputs can be prevented even on locally deployed or fine-tuned diffusion models without disabling the model or sacrificing its capabilities. A third-party regulator can enforce safety across a distributed ecosystem where the original creator no longer has direct access.

563.bp: Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove you know something—a password, a transaction's legitimacy, a secret—without revealing the secret itself. They're the backbone of privacy-preserving systems, secure voting, cryptocurrencies, and confidential computing. But there are many ways to build them, and each way trades speed for security, or proof size for verification time. Choosing the right one requires understanding real-world performance, not just theory.
563.wh: Textbooks describe zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs abstractly. SNARKs are fast to generate and create tiny proofs, but they require a trusted setup (some entity has to generate secret parameters without leaking them) and aren't resilient to quantum computers. STARKs have no trusted setup and are quantum-safe, but they generate huge proofs and are slower to make. Which one is actually better in practice? The answer depends on execution details, hardware, and real deployment constraints—none of which are clear from theory alone.
563.ap: This work implements both systems from reference code and runs them head-to-head on real hardware (consumer ARM processors, not theoretical machines). It measures proof generation time, verification speed, proof size, and traces which parts of the code consume the most CPU cycles. These measurements reveal where each system spends its effort and why.
563.ww: Implementation reveals truth that theory hides. Theory says both are 'feasible,' but real hardware shows vast differences: SNARKs are 68 times faster at proof generation, produce 123 times smaller proofs, but verify slower and demand trusted setup. STARKs are slower to build but faster to verify and quantum-safe. The CPU profiling identifies which operations dominate, giving protocol designers concrete targets for optimization.
563.po: Developers can now choose proof systems with data in hand. If you need fast proof generation and small size and have a trusted-setup infrastructure, SNARKs win. If you need verification speed, quantum safety, and transparency, STARKs are the call. For privacy-critical applications like blockchain or anonymous voting, this guidance matters because the wrong choice leaks performance and blocks scalability.

564.bp: Mental healthcare has a massive access problem. There are fewer therapists than people who need therapy, and even where therapists exist, therapy is expensive and stigmatized. If an AI system could assist therapists—handling intake, suggesting treatment approaches, providing evidence-based responses—it could extend a therapist's reach and free them to focus on the hardest cases. The key is not replacing therapists but amplifying them.
564.wh: Large language models are fluent and confident, which is dangerous in clinical settings. They can sound authoritative while being confidently wrong, they can miss subtle psychological signals, and they lack the embodied experience of being human. Small models are often dismissed as too weak for complex reasoning, but they're faster, more trustworthy to domain experts, and easier to audit. The challenge is building a small model that exhibits genuine therapeutic competence, not just fluent mimicry.
564.ap: This system takes a small language model and equips it with three tools. First, domain-specific fine-tuning on clinical data teaches it therapeutic language and psychology. Second, retrieval augmentation—the system can look up relevant clinical knowledge, guidelines, and case evidence when answering—keeps it grounded in facts instead of confabulation. Third, agentic reasoning—it can break complex clinical questions into steps and combine different tools to answer them thoroughly. The system was then evaluated by actual clinicians using novel metrics (T-BARS rubric) that measure empathy and therapeutic consistency, plus traditional safety checks.
564.ww: Small models benefit from three boosts: fine-tuning grounds them in domain knowledge, retrieval keeps them factual and current, and agentic reasoning lets them handle complexity without being large. Because the model is small, clinicians can understand what it's doing and catch errors more easily. The combination lets the small model punch above its weight: it's fast to run, auditable, and trustworthy while still giving expert-like, empathetic responses.
564.po: Actual clinical experts deployed and tested this system and confirmed it generates accurate, safe, and empathetic responses. It can now support real therapists in real mental healthcare settings, extending their capacity without replacing them—exactly what the access crisis demands.

565.bp: Financial fraud hides in transaction networks. A person who looks normal on their own—regular deposits, modest withdrawals—becomes suspicious when you see their network: they're connected to known money launderers, their patterns mirror other fraudsters. Fraud detection is a network problem: you must spot when someone's behavior is normal individually but anomalous in context. Traditional detection looks at isolated transactions; graph methods see the full picture.
565.wh: Graph methods work well on clean, balanced data, but real financial networks are catastrophically imbalanced: 99.99% of transactions are legitimate, 0.01% are fraud. Rare cases dominate learning. Second, fraud is camouflage: criminals study legitimate patterns and mimic them so they blend in. A neural network might see a fraudulent transaction and think 'this looks exactly like a normal transaction' because the fraud is deliberately disguised. Simple graph models miss this problem.
565.ap: This system is inspired by how the hippocampus in a brain detects when something's wrong—it notices conflicts and inconsistencies, not just surface similarity. The model has two modules. First, a cross-view inconsistency perception module watches transactions from multiple angles: who's involved, how much money, what time, what device. It finds subtle contradictions—'this transaction looks normal in isolation but clashes with this person's typical patterns'—that signal camouflaged fraud. Second, a novelty-aware hypergraph learning module measures how much each transaction deviates from what its neighbors would expect. If you usually transfer money to friends but suddenly transfer to a stranger, that deviation is the alarm.
565.ww: By monitoring cross-view conflicts, the system catches fraud that mimics legitimate behavior locally but breaks patterns when you zoom out. By measuring deviation from neighborhood expectations rather than global statistics, it avoids the rare-event problem: it's looking for 'does this transaction fit with who you are,' not 'is this transaction common.' Neuroscience inspiration gives the method intuitive grounding.
565.po: Fraud detection becomes more sensitive to camouflaged cases while still catching long-tailed fraud. Financial institutions can deploy this to catch fraudsters who deliberately study and mimic legitimate patterns, improving their defense against sophisticated attacks.

566.bp: When you scroll through TikTok or Amazon, you're not the same person hour by hour or week by week. Your mood shifts, your needs change, you discover new interests. Recommendation systems that treat you as a fixed preference vector miss this: they see you want books one day and recipes the next, but they can't model that as evolving interest, only as noise or contradiction. Capturing interest as a living, dynamic process is the real challenge.
566.wh: Traditional systems assume interests change in discrete jumps or follow simple linear trends. Reality is messier: you might gradually drift toward a new interest, then suddenly spike, then plateau. You might oscillate between multiple interests. And your trajectory isn't independent of the content: content you see influences where you drift next. Modeling all of this while handling multimodal data (text, images, video) at scale is complex. Existing methods use rigid diffusion models that treat interest as random drift, or they use redundant neural architectures (twin networks) that waste computation.
566.ap: This system models user interest as a continuous-time stochastic process—think of it as a particle moving through a space of possible interests, pulled by attraction to meaningful content and pushed by randomness. Instead of random drift, it uses directed drift toward the content you care about. The motion happens in multiple dimensions simultaneously (time dimension and relational dimension: how you relate to each item). A hypergraph encoder captures user-item interactions at multiple scales simultaneously, and a unified solver computes trajectories in this multi-dimensional space. Instead of redundant twin networks, the system uses a generative-discriminative co-optimization: one part generates your likely trajectory, another part checks how good the recommendations are, and they help each other in the same parameter space.
566.ww: Directed drift captures the intuition that you don't wander randomly through interests—you're pulled toward content that resonates. Stochastic differential equations let the system model smooth evolution with realistic noise. By encoding interactions at multiple scales, the system sees both your immediate circle of interests and your broader category preferences. The co-optimization trick reduces waste: you get all the reasoning in a single pass instead of running two separate models.
566.po: Recommendations improve because the system now predicts not just what you'll like next, but how your taste will evolve. The system can also output interpretable interest trajectories—you can see how your preference drifted over time and why the system made its recommendations, building user understanding and trust.

567.bp: False news spreads with images and videos now, not just text. A photo is edited to change its meaning, a video is clipped to mislead, and text wraps around it to amplify the lie. Detecting which multimodal posts are false requires understanding how images and text work together to create false impressions. A text-only detector misses the visual lies; an image-only detector misses the misleading text.
567.wh: Multimodal fake news is hard because forgery can hide at different levels: local forgeries (specific pixels edited in the image), global anomalies (the whole image looks wrong or out of place), and cross-modal inconsistencies (the image and text clash or the image is being misused). Traditional fusion approaches treat text and image as separate feature streams and combine them late, missing how forgeries interact across modalities. They also don't leverage knowledge about what's real—facts, entities, relationships—that could ground the detection.
567.ap: This system (SVPF-Net) has two stages. First, it optimizes visual representation by extracting both local details (where pixels are edited) and global properties (whether the image feels consistent). A dual-fusion enhancement uses weighted fusion to build a structured visual representation that captures local forgeries and global anomalies together, then uses cross-attention—a mechanism that lets image parts communicate—to connect local details to global patterns. Second, it fuses text and image modality-by-modality using high-quality semantic features and a progressive fusion strategy where each modality is weighted by how trustworthy it is in context.
567.ww: By capturing local and global visual signals and letting them interact, the system stops missing forgeries that would be obvious in isolation. By fusing modalities progressively with adaptive weighting, it doesn't force false equality: sometimes the text is the lie, sometimes the image is, and the system learns which to trust. By using semantic knowledge, it grounds detection in what's actually true, not just statistical oddities.
567.po: Fake news detection improves significantly because the system now sees both how images are manipulated and how misleading text weaponizes images. On real multimodal datasets, accuracy rises as the system stops missing sophisticated cross-modal misinformation.

568.bp: In a massive recommendation system like Amazon, millions of candidate items arrive from retrieval (broad search) and must be narrowed down to a few hundred for ranking. This pre-ranking stage is where most candidates die. The challenge: the ranking quality (which items matter most) and the computational budget (how fast you can score candidates) pull in opposite directions. Spend money scoring everything and quality is perfect but speed suffers; skim only cheap candidates and speed wins but quality crashes.
568.wh: Most pre-ranking systems treat all candidates as equivalent—they apply the same model to everything. But that's wasteful: some candidates are obviously good (you'd recommend them anyway), some are obviously bad (clear no-gos), and some are genuinely hard to judge. Throwing the same compute at easy and hard cases is like giving every student the same difficulty exam: easy students waste time, hard students fail to show their real ability. Additionally, training on mixed data causes gradient conflicts: the hard cases create noisy gradients that contradict the easy cases, and together they pull the model in conflicting directions.
568.ap: This system (HAP) disentangles the candidates first: identify which ones are easy to judge (the system is confident about them) and which are hard (the system is uncertain). For easy candidates, apply a fast, lightweight model—it's enough because you're already confident. For hard candidates, engage a stronger model that can do finer discrimination. Additionally, during training, direct easy and hard samples through separate optimization paths so their gradients don't collide and cancel each other. Each path has a tailored loss function that asks the right question: for easy samples, 'are you confidently correct?' for hard samples, 'are you distinguishing subtle differences?'
568.ww: By adapting computational budget to difficulty, you stop wasting inference time on trivial decisions. By separating gradient paths, you let each sample type drive optimization in the direction that helps it most. The combination preserves accuracy on hard cases while accelerating easy cases, a win-win that's only possible when you stop treating all candidates as identical.
568.po: Pre-ranking becomes both more accurate and faster: the system correctly identifies more subtle high-value candidates without bogging down on obvious cases. At scale in billion-candidate systems, this means higher-quality recommendations per millisecond of compute.

569.bp: A new restaurant opens. It's not yet well-known, so few people order it. Recommending it to more people is good for the restaurant's growth but risky: if you send the wrong people to it, you hurt its reputation. A billion items launch every day on Alibaba; most never gain traction. The challenge is to boost exposure for cold items strategically—not randomly to everyone, but to users most likely to genuinely enjoy them so their engagement sparks organic growth.
569.wh: Click-through rate (CTR) optimization alone—pick users most likely to click—seems right, but it's myopic. A user might click an item because it's 'interesting' but never buy or recommend it to friends. Their click dies in isolation. Meanwhile, another user clicks more slowly but tells ten friends, each of whom tells ten more. Long-term growth requires predicting not just 'will they click' but 'will this person's engagement generate follow-on traffic?' This counterfactual question—'if we show them this item, will other people now see it organically?'—is hard to answer.
569.ap: AliBoostV2 splits the problem. First, a Growth Potential Prediction module uses counterfactual reasoning: it models 'if I show this user this item, how much additional natural traffic will that interaction generate?' Not through their own future clicks, but through the ripple effect: they share it, people see it, some try it, the algorithm picks it up and shows it to more people. Second, a Dynamic CTR-Growth Boosting strategy targets users where both signals align: users who are likely to click (immediate signal) and users whose engagement will trigger cascading organic visibility (growth signal). It also adapts across time: users' behavior varies by hour or day, so targeting also varies dynamically.
569.ww: Counterfactual reasoning lets the system predict the ripple effect: not just whether a user will click, but whether their click starts a cascade. By optimizing for both CTR and growth simultaneously, the system avoids the trap of chasing empty clicks—engagement that doesn't propagate. Dynamic adaptation means the system keeps working as user behavior shifts hourly or seasonally.
569.po: Cold-start items (new items with no history) grow much faster and more reliably. Over six months on live Alibaba and Taobao platforms, the system successfully cold-started over one billion new items by targeting growth-catalyzing users, not just clickers. Items reach viability faster and with healthier long-term engagement patterns.
